terms.text: Segment Anything Model for Medical Images

preserved_constraints.text: MedSAM与nnU-Net用于医学图像分割有什么区别？

claims.text: 两者在医学图像分割中的核心区别是设计范式不同：nnU-Net 是面向每个数据集自动配置的专用（specialized）U-Net 框架，MedSAM 是以提示（bounding box）驱动、在大规模多模态医学图像上训练的通用（generalist）基础模型；一项比较研究将二者分别归为专用方法与提示驱动通用方法，并报告二者在精度、数据需求和实用性上存在权衡。
limitations: 比较研究的摘要未给出具体数值结果，权衡方向与幅度未在证据中量化。

claims.text: nnU-Net 基于 2D 和 3D 原生 U-Net，主张去除多余网络设计，转而自动适配架构、预处理、训练和推理等自由度；其在医学分割十项全能挑战中不允许数据集间人工调整，并在提交时于七个第一阶段任务上取得最高平均 Dice（BrainTumour 第 1 类除外）。
limitations: 证据为摘要，未提供各任务具体 Dice 数值与配置细节。

claims.text: MedSAM 是面向通用医学图像分割的基础模型，在含 1,570,263 个图像-掩码对、覆盖 10 种成像模态和 30 余种癌症类型的大规模数据集上开发，并在 86 个内部和 60 个外部验证任务上评估，报告其精度与稳健性优于按模态划分的专家模型。
limitations: 该结论来自摘要，未给出具体指标数值。

claims.text: MedSAM 的网络基于 transformer：ViT-base 图像编码器提取特征，提示编码器将用户交互（边界框）映射为嵌入，轻量 mask decoder 融合图像与提示嵌入并输出分割结果与置信度；输入为 1024×1024×3，图像嵌入为 64×64。
limitations: 来自全文 Methods/Network architecture 部分，未涉及训练数据之外的泛化表现。

claims.text: 现有证据仅支持定性比较：比较研究指出专用与通用模型在精度、数据需求和实际可用性之间存在权衡，并考察了模型稳健性、对提示设计的敏感性、无额外训练时的泛化性以及体积上下文的影响；但未检索到给出 MedSAM 与 nnU-Net 直接数值对比的段落。
limitations: 比较研究仅有摘要，具体数据集、指标与结果未在证据中呈现。

claims.text: 由于 MedSAM 与 nnU-Net 的评估设置不同（MedSAM 为 86 个内部与 60 个外部任务、多模态大规模训练；nnU-Net 为十项全能挑战七项任务、无数据集间人工调整），不能从这些证据直接汇总或推断二者的优劣。
limitations: 该推断基于评估设置差异，非直接对照实验。

openalex_record.title: nnU-Net: Self-adapting Framework for U-Net-Based Medical Image Segmentation
openalex_record.abstract: The U-Net was presented in 2015. With its straight-forward and successful architecture it quickly evolved to a commonly used benchmark in medical image segmentation. The adaptation of the U-Net to novel problems, however, comprises several degrees of freedom regarding the exact architecture, preprocessing, training and inference. These choices are not independent of each other and substantially impact the overall performance. The present paper introduces the nnU-Net ('no-new-Net'), which refers to a robust and self-adapting framework on the basis of 2D and 3D vanilla U-Nets. We argue the strong case for taking away superfluous bells and whistles of many proposed network designs and instead focus on the remaining aspects that make out the performance and generalizability of a method. We evaluate the nnU-Net in the context of the Medical Segmentation Decathlon challenge, which measures segmentation performance in ten disciplines comprising distinct entities, image modalities, image geometries and dataset sizes, with no manual adjustments between datasets allowed. At the time of manuscript submission, nnU-Net achieves the highest mean dice scores across all classes and seven phase 1 tasks (except class 1 in BrainTumour) in the online leaderboard of the challenge.

sources.title: nnU-Net: Self-adapting Framework for U-Net-Based Medical Image Segmentation

evidence.text: The U-Net was presented in 2015. With its straight-forward and successful architecture it quickly evolved to a commonly used benchmark in medical image segmentation. The adaptation of the U-Net to novel problems, however, comprises several degrees of freedom regarding the exact architecture, preprocessing, training and inference. These choices are not independent of each other and substantially impact the overall performance. The present paper introduces the nnU-Net ('no-new-Net'), which refers to a robust and self-adapting framework on the basis of 2D and 3D vanilla U-Nets. We argue the strong case for taking away superfluous bells and whistles of many proposed network designs and instead focus on the remaining aspects that make out the performance and generalizability of a method. We evaluate the nnU-Net in the context of the Medical Segmentation Decathlon challenge, which measures segmentation performance in ten disciplines comprising distinct entities, image modalities, image geometries and dataset sizes, with no manual adjustments between datasets allowed. At the time of manuscript submission, nnU-Net achieves the highest mean dice scores across all classes and seven phase 1 tasks (except class 1 in BrainTumour) in the online leaderboard of the challenge.

openalex_record.title: Segment anything in medical images
openalex_record.abstract: Medical image segmentation is a critical component in clinical practice, facilitating accurate diagnosis, treatment planning, and disease monitoring. However, existing methods, often tailored to specific modalities or disease types, lack generalizability across the diverse spectrum of medical image segmentation tasks. Here we present MedSAM, a foundation model designed for bridging this gap by enabling universal medical image segmentation. The model is developed on a large-scale medical image dataset with 1,570,263 image-mask pairs, covering 10 imaging modalities and over 30 cancer types. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation on 86 internal validation tasks and 60 external validation tasks, demonstrating better accuracy and robustness than modality-wise specialist models. By delivering accurate and efficient segmentation across a wide spectrum of tasks, MedSAM holds significant potential to expedite the evolution of diagnostic tools and the personalization of treatment plans.

evidence.text: Medical image segmentation is a critical component in clinical practice, facilitating accurate diagnosis, treatment planning, and disease monitoring. However, existing methods, often tailored to specific modalities or disease types, lack generalizability across the diverse spectrum of medical image segmentation tasks. Here we present MedSAM, a foundation model designed for bridging this gap by enabling universal medical image segmentation. The model is developed on a large-scale medical image dataset with 1,570,263 image-mask pairs, covering 10 imaging modalities and over 30 cancer types. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation on 86 internal validation tasks and 60 external validation tasks, demonstrating better accuracy and robustness than modality-wise specialist models. By delivering accurate and efficient segmentation across a wide spectrum of tasks, MedSAM holds significant potential to expedite the evolution of diagnostic tools and the personalization of treatment plans.

fulltext.text: The network utilized in this study was built on transformer architecture27, which has demonstrated remarkable effectiveness in various domains such as natural language processing and image recognition tasks25. Specifically, the network incorporated a vision transformer (ViT)-based image encoder responsible for extracting image features, a prompt encoder for integrating user interactions (bounding boxes), and a mask decoder that generated segmentation results and confidence scores using the image embedding, prompt embedding, and output token.

fulltext.title: Segment anything in medical images
fulltext.text: To strike a balance between segmentation performance and computational efficiency, we employed the base ViT model as the image encoder since extensive evaluation indicated that larger ViT models, such as ViT Large and ViT Huge, offered only marginal improvements in accuracy7 while significantly increasing computational demands. Specifically, the base ViT model consists of 12 transformer layers27, with each block comprising a multi-head self-attention block and a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) block incorporating layer normalization35. Pre-training was performed using masked auto-encoder modeling36, followed by fully supervised training on the SAM dataset7. The input image (1024 × 1024 × 3) was reshaped into a sequence of flattened 2D patches with the size 16 × 16 × 3, yielding a feature size in image embedding of 64 × 64 after passing through the image encoder, which is 16 × downscaled. The prompt encoders mapped the corner point of the bounding box prompt to 256-dimensional vectorial embeddings26. In particular, each bounding box was represented by an embedding pair of the top-left corner point and the bottom-right corner point.

fulltext.text: To facilitate real-time user interactions once the image embedding had been computed, a lightweight mask decoder architecture was employed. It consists of two transformer layers27 for fusing the image embedding and prompt encoding, and two transposed convolutional layers to enhance the embedding resolution to 256 × 256. Subsequently, the embedding underwent sigmoid activation, followed by bi-linear interpolations to match the input size.

openalex_record.title: Modern tools for medical image segmentation
openalex_record.journal: Brno University of Technology Digital Library (Brno University of Technology)
openalex_record.abstract: Segmentace medicínských obrazů představuje základní krok v počítačem podporované diagnostice a klinickém výzkumu. Tato práce srovnává specializované a generalistické přístupy k segmentaci medicínských obrazů, přičemž porovnává framework nnU-Net s~generalistickými modely řízenými prompty, jako jsou MedSAM a BiomedParse. Hodnocení zahrnuje více zobrazovacích modalit a anatomických struktur s využitím veřejně dostupných datasetů. Jsou provedeny cílené experimenty zaměřené na robustnost modelů, citlivost na design promptů, zobecnitelnost bez dodatečného trénování a vliv volumetrického kontextu na kvalitu segmentace. Výsledky poukazují na kompromisy mezi specializovanými a generalistickými modely z hlediska přesnosti, datových požadavků a praktické použitelnosti a identifikují klíčové faktory relevantní pro klinické nasazení.

evidence.text: Segmentace medicínských obrazů představuje základní krok v počítačem podporované diagnostice a klinickém výzkumu. Tato práce srovnává specializované a generalistické přístupy k segmentaci medicínských obrazů, přičemž porovnává framework nnU-Net s~generalistickými modely řízenými prompty, jako jsou MedSAM a BiomedParse. Hodnocení zahrnuje více zobrazovacích modalit a anatomických struktur s využitím veřejně dostupných datasetů. Jsou provedeny cílené experimenty zaměřené na robustnost modelů, citlivost na design promptů, zobecnitelnost bez dodatečného trénování a vliv volumetrického kontextu na kvalitu segmentace. Výsledky poukazují na kompromisy mezi specializovanými a generalistickými modely z hlediska přesnosti, datových požadavků a praktické použitelnosti a identifikují klíčové faktory relevantní pro klinické nasazení.

assessments.quote: The present paper introduces the nnU-Net ('no-new-Net'), which refers to a robust and self-adapting framework on the basis of 2D and 3D vanilla U-Nets.
assessments.reason: Original nnU-Net framework paper for medical image segmentation; describes self-adapting design and evaluation on Medical Segmentation Decathlon. Direct evidence for the nnU-Net side of the comparison.

assessments.quote: We propose the Medical SAM Adapter (Med-SA), which is one of the first methods to integrate SAM into medical image segmentation.
assessments.reason: Adapts SAM (not MedSAM specifically) for medical segmentation; relevant to SAM-based approaches but does not address MedSAM vs nnU-Net comparison.

assessments.quote: Here we present MedSAM, a foundation model designed for bridging this gap by enabling universal medical image segmentation.
assessments.reason: Original MedSAM paper; describes foundation-model design, large-scale training data and evaluation across many tasks. Direct evidence for the MedSAM side.

assessments.quote: Tato práce srovnává specializované a generalistické přístupy k segmentaci medicínských obrazů, přičemž porovnává framework nnU-Net s~generalistickými modely řízenými prompty, jako jsou MedSAM a BiomedParse.
assessments.reason: Directly compares nnU-Net with MedSAM across modalities, examining robustness, prompt sensitivity, generalizability and accuracy trade-offs. Covers the comparison dimensions.

assessments.quote: We introduce SCORE (Segmentation COrrection from Regional Evaluations), a weakly supervised framework that refines automated segmentations using simple regional visual assessments instead of fully annotated reference masks.
assessments.reason: Segmentation correction for humerus CT; does not involve MedSAM or nnU-Net comparison.

assessments.quote: Tumor multi-region segmentation was conducted using nnU-Net, followed by extraction of VASARI features and ADC-related parameters.
assessments.reason: nnU-Net used only as a preprocessing tool for downstream glioma subtype prediction; not a MedSAM vs nnU-Net segmentation comparison.

assessments.quote: we utilize a so-called U-net, which relies on large amounts of labeled radar data for training.
assessments.reason: Weather radar echo removal using U-net; not medical image segmentation and not MedSAM/nnU-Net.

assessments.quote: In this study, we perform a boundary-aware analysis of deep learning-based knee MRI segmentation using multiple evaluation metrics, including Dice, HD95, and ASSD.
assessments.reason: Boundary-aware evaluation of knee MRI segmentation; does not compare MedSAM and nnU-Net.

assessments.quote: We implemented a fully convolutional 3D dose‐prediction model adapted from the MedNeXt architecture
assessments.reason: Radiotherapy dose prediction, not segmentation, and no MedSAM/nnU-Net comparison.

assessments.quote: a novel HCSA-RMSDC U-Net is designed in this work, which is characterized by an asymmetric architecture with a computationally heavy encoder and a lightweight decoder.
assessments.reason: Custom U-Net variant for brain tumor segmentation; does not involve MedSAM or nnU-Net comparison.

assessments.quote: We propose SAMed, a general solution for medical image segmentation.
assessments.reason: This is a SAM-based (SAMed) medical segmentation method, related to the MedSAM family of SAM customization but not MedSAM itself, and it does not address nnU-Net or a comparison. Useful indirect evidence for SAM-based approaches only.

assessments.quote: Thermal perfusion imaging is feasible using the novel implemented deep learning system.
assessments.reason: Thermal perfusion mapping of foot microcirculation during revascularization; not a MedSAM vs nnU-Net medical image segmentation comparison.

assessments.quote: We developed a dual-decoder 3D BiFormer-UNet for humerus and scapula segmentation and heatmap-based localization of 14 anatomical landmarks.
assessments.reason: Landmark detection with a custom BiFormer-UNet; does not involve MedSAM or nnU-Net or their comparison.

records.title: nnU-Net: Self-adapting Framework for U-Net-Based Medical Image Segmentation
records.abstract: The U-Net was presented in 2015. With its straight-forward and successful architecture it quickly evolved to a commonly used benchmark in medical image segmentation. The adaptation of the U-Net to novel problems, however, comprises several degrees of freedom regarding the exact architecture, preprocessing, training and inference. These choices are not independent of each other and substantially impact the overall performance. The present paper introduces the nnU-Net ('no-new-Net'), which refers to a robust and self-adapting framework on the basis of 2D and 3D vanilla U-Nets. We argue the strong case for taking away superfluous bells and whistles of many proposed network designs and instead focus on the remaining aspects that make out the performance and generalizability of a method. We evaluate the nnU-Net in the context of the Medical Segmentation Decathlon challenge, which measures segmentation performance in ten disciplines comprising distinct entities, image modalities, image geometries and dataset sizes, with no manual adjustments between datasets allowed. At the time of manuscript submission, nnU-Net achieves the highest mean dice scores across all classes and seven phase 1 tasks (except class 1 in BrainTumour) in the online leaderboard of the challenge.

records.title: nnU-Net: Breaking the Spell on Successful Medical Image Segmentation.
records.abstract:
Fueled by the diversity of datasets, semantic segmentation is a popular
subfield in medical image analysis with a vast number of new methods being
proposed each year. This ever-growing jungle of methodologies, however, becomes
increasingly impenetrable. At the same time, many proposed methods fail to
generalize beyond the experiments they were demonstrated on, thus hampering the
process of developing a segmentation algorithm on a new dataset. Here we
present nnU-Net ('no-new-Net'), a framework that automatically adapts itself to
any given new dataset. While this process was completely human-driven so far,
we make a first attempt to automate necessary adaptations such as
preprocessing, the exact patch size, batch size, and inference settings based
on the properties of a given dataset. Remarkably, nnU-Net strips away the
architectural bells and whistles that are typically proposed in the literature
and relies on just a simple U-Net architecture embedded in a robust training
scheme. Out of the box, nnU-Net achieves state of the art performance on six
well-established segmentation challenges. Source code is available at
https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/nnunet.

records.title: Medical SAM adapter: Adapting segment anything model for medical image segmentation
records.abstract: The Segment Anything Model (SAM) has recently gained popularity in the field of image segmentation due to its impressive capabilities in various segmentation tasks and its prompt-based interface. However, recent studies and individual experiments have shown that SAM underperforms in medical image segmentation due to the lack of medical-specific knowledge. This raises the question of how to enhance SAM's segmentation capability for medical images. We propose the Medical SAM Adapter (Med-SA), which is one of the first methods to integrate SAM into medical image segmentation. Med-SA uses a light yet effective adaptation technique instead of fine-tuning the SAM model, incorporating domain-specific medical knowledge into the segmentation model. We also propose Space-Depth Transpose (SD-Trans) to adapt 2D SAM to 3D medical images and Hyper-Prompting Adapter (HyP-Adpt) to achieve prompt-conditioned adaptation. Comprehensive evaluation experiments on 17 medical image segmentation tasks across various modalities demonstrate the superior performance of Med-SA while updating only 2% of the SAM parameters (13M). records.title: Customized Segment Anything Model for Medical Image Segmentation
records.abstract: We propose SAMed, a general solution for medical image segmentation. Different from the previous methods, SAMed is built upon the large-scale image segmentation model, Segment Anything Model (SAM), to explore the new research paradigm of customizing large-scale models for medical image segmentation. SAMed applies the low-rank-based (LoRA) finetuning strategy to the SAM image encoder and finetunes it together with the prompt encoder and the mask decoder on labeled medical image segmentation datasets. We also observe the warmup finetuning strategy and the AdamW optimizer lead SAMed to successful convergence and lower loss. Different from SAM, SAMed could perform semantic segmentation on medical images. Our trained SAMed model achieves 81.88 DSC and 20.64 HD on the Synapse multi-organ segmentation dataset, which is on par with the state-of-the-art methods. We conduct extensive experiments to validate the effectiveness of our design. Since SAMed only updates a small fraction of the SAM parameters, its deployment cost and storage cost are quite marginal in practical usage. The code of SAMed is available at https://github.com/hitachinsk/SAMed.

records.title: Segment anything in medical images
records.abstract: Medical image segmentation is a critical component in clinical practice, facilitating accurate diagnosis, treatment planning, and disease monitoring. However, existing methods, often tailored to specific modalities or disease types, lack generalizability across the diverse spectrum of medical image segmentation tasks. Here we present MedSAM, a foundation model designed for bridging this gap by enabling universal medical image segmentation. The model is developed on a large-scale medical image dataset with 1,570,263 image-mask pairs, covering 10 imaging modalities and over 30 cancer types. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation on 86 internal validation tasks and 60 external validation tasks, demonstrating better accuracy and robustness than modality-wise specialist models. By delivering accurate and efficient segmentation across a wide spectrum of tasks, MedSAM holds significant potential to expedite the evolution of diagnostic tools and the personalization of treatment plans.

records.title: Modern tools for medical image segmentation
records.journal: Brno University of Technology Digital Library (Brno University of Technology)
records.abstract: Segmentace medicínských obrazů představuje základní krok v počítačem podporované diagnostice a klinickém výzkumu. Tato práce srovnává specializované a generalistické přístupy k segmentaci medicínských obrazů, přičemž porovnává framework nnU-Net s~generalistickými modely řízenými prompty, jako jsou MedSAM a BiomedParse. Hodnocení zahrnuje více zobrazovacích modalit a anatomických struktur s využitím veřejně dostupných datasetů. Jsou provedeny cílené experimenty zaměřené na robustnost modelů, citlivost na design promptů, zobecnitelnost bez dodatečného trénování a vliv volumetrického kontextu na kvalitu segmentace. Výsledky poukazují na kompromisy mezi specializovanými a generalistickými modely z hlediska přesnosti, datových požadavků a praktické použitelnosti a identifikují klíčové faktory relevantní pro klinické nasazení.

records.title: Correction automatique de segmentations pour la planification chirurgicale par apprentissage faiblement supervisé
records.abstract: Accurate humerus segmentation in CT images is essential for 3D preoperative planning, yet automated methods remain prone to errors. We introduce SCORE (Segmentation COrrection from Regional Evaluations), a weakly supervised framework that refines automated segmentations using simple regional visual assessments instead of fully annotated reference masks. SCORE employs a 3D U-Net trained with a novel morphology-constrained loss function to translate regional quality scores and error labels into voxel-level corrections. Evaluated on three datasets covering complete, proximal, and distal humeri, SCORE significantly improved segmentation accuracy. On complete humeri, Dice increased from 92.4% to 96.2%, while the 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance decreased from 2.1 to 1.4 mm. Performance was comparable to fully supervised methods, while requiring only 4 minutes of visual assessment per scan, representing a 95% reduction in annotation time. SCORE offers an efficient approach to improving automated segmentation reliability for clinical applications.

records.title: Application of a Fusion Model Combining MRI-VASARI Features and ADC in Predicting the Molecular Subtypes of Adult-type Diffuse Gliomas
records.journal: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
records.abstract: Objective: To develop a machine learning model integrating MRI visually accessible Rembrandt images (VASARI) features and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) parameters for the preoperative classification of the three subtypes of adult-type diffuse glioma. Methods: This study retrospectively enrolled 206 patients with pathologically confirmed adult-type diffuse glioma and divided them by scanner type into a training set (n=114) and an independent validation set (n=92). Tumor multi-region segmentation was conducted using nnU-Net, followed by extraction of VASARI features and ADC-related parameters. Recursive feature elimination with cross-validation (RFECV), XGBoost feature importance ranking, and incremental feature selection were applied to identify the optimal feature subset, and an XGBoost-based multiclass fusion model was subsequently constructed. Results: Twelve VASARI features and four ADC parameters (ADCmin, ADCmean, rADCmin, and rADCmean) differed significantly among the three subtypes. Eight features were finally selected for model construction. The fusion model achieved accuracies of 96.49% in the training set and 80.43% in the validation set. In the validation cohort, the area under the curves (AUCs) for predicting astrocytoma and glioblastoma were 0.96 and 0.97, respectively, both higher than those of the standalone VASARI and ADC models, while the AUC for oligodendroglioma was 0.59. SHAP analysis revealed that diffusion restriction, ADC parameters, and the margin of the non-enhancing region were the primary contributors to the model. Conclusion: The XGBoost-based fusion model integrating MRI-VASARI features and ADC demonstrated a high diagnostic performance in distinguishing glioblastoma and astrocytoma, but its ability to differentiate oligodendroglioma remained limited. Future studies should incorporate additional imaging features, such as calcification, to further improve the model performance.

records.title: Enhancing weather radar data by removing non-meteorological echoes, using neural networks trained on synthetic weather data
records.abstract: Abstract. Meteorological weather radars are essential for atmospheric research, weather forecasting and aviation safety, but they often detect non-meteorological echoes from scatterers such as insects, birds, and ground clutter. These non-meteorological echoes can then lead to misinterpretations in quantitative precipitation estimation and hydrometeor classification, which cause difficulties for atmospheric research and weather forecasting. This paper introduces a novel AI-based approach to identify such non-meteorological echoes in polarimetric radar data using a convolutional neural network. More specifically, we utilize a so-called U-net, which relies on large amounts of labeled radar data for training. To address the challenge of acquiring labeled radar data consisting of meteorological and non-meteorological echoes, we generate synthetic training samples by combining preprocessed winter data (meteorological echoes) with cluttered summer data (non-meteorological echoes) provided by Deutscher Wetterdienst (DWD). After training on synthetic data, evaluation of the U-net approach on operationally measured radar data shows that it outperforms the state-of-the-art DWD classification algorithm overall. This is particularly evident in the preservation of precipitation signals at the boundaries of larger weather events.

records.title: Beyond dice: boundary-aware analysis for knee MRI segmentation
records.journal: International Conference on Image Processing, Object Detection, and Tracking (IPODT)
records.abstract: Accurate knee MRI segmentation plays an important role in cartilage assessment and osteoarthritis analysis. Existing deep learning studies mainly focus on improving overlap-based metrics such as the Dice coefficient, while the reliability of segmentation boundaries is often insufficiently investigated. However, many knee cartilage structures exhibit thin and complex boundaries, where small boundary deviations may lead to clinically relevant errors despite only marginal changes in Dice scores. In this study, we perform a boundary-aware analysis of deep learning-based knee MRI segmentation using multiple evaluation metrics, including Dice, HD95, and ASSD. Quantitative comparison, metric correlation analysis, organ-wise evaluation, and failure case visualization are conducted to investigate the inconsistency between overlap-based and boundary-based assessment. Experimental results demonstrate that models with comparable Dice scores may still exhibit substantially different boundary behaviors. In particular, several high-Dice cases still present severe boundary deviations, indicating that overlap-based metrics alone may fail to fully characterize segmentation quality. Furthermore, thin cartilage structures are shown to be more sensitive to boundary instability than larger anatomical regions. These findings suggest that Dice alone is insufficient for comprehensive evaluation of knee MRI segmentation performance. Boundary-sensitive metrics provide complementary information that is essential for reliable assessment of medical image segmentation models.

records.title: A generalizable 3D dose prediction across heterogeneous cohorts: A framework developed for the 2025 AAPM GDP‐HMM challenge
records.abstract: Abstract Background Manual radiotherapy treatment planning is labor‐intensive, subjective, and highly variable across planners and institutions. Deep learning has emerged as a promising approach for estimating achievable three‐dimensional (3D) dose distributions for a given plan (hereafter: dose prediction) by directly mapping patient anatomy and beam geometry to voxel‐wise dose. However, achieving robust generalization across diverse anatomical sites, prescriptions, and institutions remains a major challenge, particularly under computational constraints required for clinical deployment. Purpose We sought to develop and evaluate a generalizable, computationally efficient 3D dose prediction framework capable of spanning heterogeneous multi‐site and multi‐cohort datasets, as defined in the 2025 AAPM Generalizable Dose Prediction for Heterogeneous Multi‐Cohort and Multi‐Site (GDP‐HMM) Grand Challenge. Our goal was to design a model that not only achieved state‐of‐the‐art voxel‐wise accuracy but also maintained clinically meaningful dose‐volume and geometric characteristics across diverse cases. Methods We implemented a fully convolutional 3D dose‐prediction model adapted from the MedNeXt architecture, which was originally introduced as a high‐capacity convolutional backbone for medical image segmentation and is well suited to volumetric dense prediction tasks. The network accepted multimodal inputs comprising CT, PTV/OAR masks, beam and angle plates, and scalar plan metadata. A composite loss function combined voxel‐wise L 1 , body‐masked weighted L 1 , structure‐wise moment‐matching, and gradient‐based penalties to jointly preserve spatial fidelity and dosimetric accuracy. The model was trained on the fixed GDP‐HMM dataset consisting of 2876 training plans, 356 validation plans, and a held‐out test set of 498 plans using random 3D patches and evaluated by mean absolute error (MAE), homogeneity index (HI), and conformity indices (CI100%, CI50%). Ablation studies quantified the contribution of each loss component to overall performance. Statistical comparisons used paired Wilcoxon tests with false discovery rate correction. Results The proposed model achieved a mean voxel‐wise MAE of 2.04 Gy on the validation set, outperforming the challenge baseline (2.54 Gy). An ensemble with the baseline further improved MAE to 1.94 Gy on the validation set and 2.071 Gy on the held‐out test set, corresponding to the lowest test‐set MAE and first‐place overall ranking in the GDP‐HMM Challenge. Predicted dose distributions preserved key plan characteristics, with ΔHI, ΔCI 100% , and ΔCI 50% narrowly centered around zero, indicating consistent target coverage and dose conformity. Protocol‐specific evaluations for head‐and‐neck and lung cohorts demonstrated close alignment with reference plans, with no systematic degradation in OAR endpoints. Ablation experiments showed that removing gradient‐based terms increased MAE by 0.50 Gy, while excluding the moment‐matching term increased MAE by 0.06 Gy confirming that both gradient‐ and moment‐based constraints enhanced spatial and dosimetric fidelity. Conclusion We present a generalizable 3D dose prediction framework that achieves state‐of‐the‐art accuracy while satisfying stringent runtime requirements (< 3s per case on < 24 GB GPU memory). By integrating gradient‐aware and moment‐based constraints within a MedNeXt backbone, the model preserved clinical DVH endpoints and geometric plan features. These findings demonstrate that carefully engineered loss formulations are pivotal for cross‐institutional generalization. The framework offers a foundation for rapid dose prediction that could accelerate treatment planning, reduce inter‐planner variability, and enable intelligent automation in radiotherapy workflows.

records.title: Machine leaning assisted thermal reperfusion mapping reveals real-time changes in foot microcirculation during endovascular revascularisation
records.abstract: Objective To test the feasibility of a novel thermal perfusion imaging and mapping system to show microcirculatory changes of plantar foot angiosomes during endovascular procedures. Methods A prospective, exploratory MedTech development study was designed to test the system in a series of patients with chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (CLTI). Intraprocedural video thermography was performed using a 320 × 240 pixel resolution, thermal camera. Initial analysis was manual, re- positioning regions of interest (ROIs) within each of five plantar foot angiosomes. Subsequent automation using deep learning segmentation allowed ROI tracking from initial frame to procedure end. Isotherms (thermal contours) created and applied to the segmented surface provides quantitative, real-time changes in the percentage distribution of isotherms overlying both treated and contralateral foot angiosomes during the procedure. Results Of 23 participants recruited, video thermography was obtained in 21 patients admitted with moderate-severe disease complexity; femoral-popliteal segment only ( n = 13), femoral-popliteal and infrapopliteal disease ( n = 5) and infrapopliteal disease only ( n = 3). Changes in percentage distribution of each isotherm overlay revealed two broad groups; plantar foot thermal perfusion responders ( n = 12) and non-responders ( n = 9). In responders, revascularisation led to a series of ‘dynamic’ phases where temperature increased in one, or more, angiosomes; ‘hottest’ isotherms expanded significantly ( p = .002) in response to endovascular procedures. In thermal perfusion non-responders, no significant change in isotherm percentage distribution was observed. Conclusion Thermal perfusion imaging is feasible using the novel implemented deep learning system. Clinicians can gain insight about microcirculatory changes at foot angiosomes in response to treatment based on three parameters; (i) temporal temperature profiles of each angiosome, (ii) real-time changes in the percentage distribution of isotherms across the plantar surface during the intervention, (iii) angiosome-specific cutaneous perfusion responses to balloon inflation and/or stent deployment. For patients with diabetes, locating the site of improved skin reperfusion has potential to predict treatment success for healing outcomes at the ulcer/woundosome

records.title: Asymmetric encoder-decoder U-net with hybrid attention and residual dilated convolution for brain tumor segmentation
records.abstract: Inroduction The accurate and automatic segmentation of brain tumors from magnetic resonance imaging is regarded as essential for clinical diagnosis and surgical planning. Nevertheless, the concurrent extraction of both local fine details and global contextual cues remains challenging, primarily due to ambiguous tumor margins and marked disparities in tumor dimensions. Methods To address these issues, a novel HCSA-RMSDC U-Net is designed in this work, which is characterized by an asymmetric architecture with a computationally heavy encoder and a lightweight decoder. Specifically, a hybrid channel–spatial attention (HCSA) module is incorporated into the encoder, wherein axial decomposed convolution is utilized to capture directional spatial information, thereby enhancing spatial feature representation for tumor segmentation. Concurrently, a residual multi-scale dilated convolution (RMSDC) module is deployed in the bottleneck layer to capture semantic information across varying scales without increasing the spatial resolution. Results The proposed model was evaluated on the publicly available BRISC 2025 and Figshare datasets, achieving Dice coefficients of 87.39% and 82.84%, respectively Discussion These findings support the complementary roles of the HCSA and RMSDC mechanisms in enhancing feature representation and multi-scale contextual modeling. Overall, the proposed framework provides a fully automated approach for brain tumor segmentation.

records.title: A multi-task learning-based network for detecting three-dimensional osteometric landmarks of the shoulder joint
records.abstract: Background Mirror-based preoperative planning for total shoulder arthroplasty relies on accurate three-dimensional (3D) localization of bony landmarks on the contralateral, anatomically intact shoulder. Manual annotation is time-consuming and shows inter- and intra-observer variability. The aim of this study was to develop and evaluate a multi-task deep-learning network for automated 3D bony landmark detection on contralateral shoulder CT. Methods In this single-center retrospective study, 179 patients with intact contralateral shoulder CT scans were split at the patient level into training (n = 125), validation (n = 18), and test (n = 36) sets. We developed a dual-decoder 3D BiFormer-UNet for humerus and scapula segmentation and heatmap-based localization of 14 anatomical landmarks. A cross-task feature-fusion (CtFF) module transferred bone-structural guidance from the segmentation decoder to the landmark decoder. The network was trained end-to-end using a composite loss comprising hard-negative-mining heatmap regression, a geometric structure constraint, distance-aware similarity learning, and auxiliary segmentation loss. Landmark localization was evaluated using MRE and SDR at thresholds of 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, and 4.0 mm, while segmentation was assessed using the Dice coefficient. Per-case MRE was compared with four 3D baseline models using paired tests with Holm–Bonferroni correction. Results In the 36-case test set, the proposed model achieved an MRE of 2.1 ± 1.2 mm (95% CI, 1.7–2.5 mm) and SDRs of 72.0%, 81.8%, 90.3%, and 96.7% at thresholds of 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, and 4.0 mm, respectively. Its MRE was significantly lower than those of 3D U-Net, V-Net, 3D HRNet adaptation, and H3DE-Net (all Holm–Bonferroni-adjusted P < 0.05). On the test set, the auxiliary segmentation branch achieved mean Dice coefficients of 0.83 ± 0.05 for the humerus and 0.78 ± 0.07 for the scapula. Internally defined center landmarks, particularly the humeral head rotation center, anatomical neck center, and proximal and distal medullary canal centers, showed larger localization errors (2.3–2.6 mm) than most surface landmarks. Conclusion The proposed multi-task framework demonstrated promising 3D landmark localization performance on intact contralateral shoulder CT by integrating global anatomical context with bone-structural guidance. It may serve as an upstream localization component for mirror-based shoulder arthroplasty planning, although external validation is required before clinical use.
